t.1.45.1: When those sons of hers had been slain, O Rāma, Diti, overwhelmed with the deepest grief, spoke these words to her husband Kāśyapa, the son of Marīci.
t.1.45.2: O blessed one, I am one whose sons have been slain by your mighty sons. I desire a son, won through long austerity, who will slay Śakra.
t.1.45.3: I, such as I am, shall practise austerities; you should grant me an embryo, a son of such a kind as to slay Śakra, and you should give your consent to it.
t.1.45.4: Having heard those words of hers, the greatly radiant Kāśyapa, son of Marīci, then replied to Diti, who was deeply grieved.
t.1.45.5: So be it, blessings upon you; remain pure, O woman rich in austerity. You will give birth to a son who will slay Śakra in battle.
t.1.45.6: But if you remain pure until a full thousand years have passed, you will bear from me a son who will be the slayer of the three worlds.
t.1.45.8: When he had gone, O best of men, Diti, supremely delighted, reached Kuśaplavana and performed most severe austerities.
t.1.45.7: Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor stroked her with his hand. Then, having touched her and said, "May it be well with you," he departed to practice austerities.
t.1.45.9: While she was performing austerities, O best of men, the thousand-eyed Sahasrākṣa attended upon her with service, endowed with the highest wealth of virtues.
t.1.45.11: At all times Śakra attended upon Diti, massaging her limbs and relieving her weariness.
t.1.45.10: Sahasrākṣa brought her fire, kuśa grass, firewood, water, fruits and roots as well, and whatever else was desired.
t.1.45.12: Then, O Raghunandana, when the thousand years were ten short of completion, Diti, supremely pleased, spoke to Sahasrākṣa.
t.1.45.13: O best of the mighty, ten years still remain for her who is practising austerity. Blessings upon you! After that you will see your brother.
t.1.45.14: For your sake, my son, I shall bring forth that one who is eager for victory, and together with him, my son, you will enjoy the conquest of the three worlds, free from anxiety.
t.1.45.15: Having spoken thus to Śakra, when the sun had reached the middle of the sky, the goddess Diti was overcome by sleep, having laid herself down with her feet where her head should have been.
t.1.45.16: Seeing her impure, with her hair laid toward the feet and her feet placed where her head should be, Śakra laughed and rejoiced.
t.1.45.17: Puraṃdara entered an opening in her body, and, O Rāma, that supremely self-possessed one split the embryo into seven parts.
t.1.45.18: Then the embryo, being split by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, cried out loudly, O Rāma, and thereupon Diti awoke.
t.1.45.19: "Do not cry, do not cry," Śakra said to the embryo; and the mighty Vāsava split it apart even as it was crying.
t.1.45.20: "He must not be killed, he must not be killed!" thus spoke Diti. Then Śakra came out, out of respect for his mother's words.
t.1.45.21: Holding his vajra and with palms joined in reverence, Śakra said to Diti: "O goddess, you are impure, for you slept with your hair lying where your feet should be."
t.1.45.22: Having found that opportunity, I split into seven parts the one who would be the slayer of Śakra in battle. O goddess, you ought to forgive me for that.
